seeds.asked: Describe the ionic bases of phase 1 and phase 2 in cardiac myocyte action potential
seeds.label: Phase 1 of the cardiac myocyte action potential is a transient potassium efflux and phase 2 a plateau that balances potassium efflux against calcium entry
seeds.definition: Phase 1 is the rapid small repolarization that follows the upstroke: transient outward potassium channels open and carry Ito, chloride enters, and the fast sodium channels inactivate. Phase 2 is the plateau, about 200 msec in a ventricular myocyte and held near zero millivolts by two opposing currents that cancel — a small outward potassium current through delayed rectifier channels, and an inward positive current made of calcium entering through long-lasting (L-type) channels together with the sodium-calcium exchanger, which moves one calcium ion out for three sodium ions in and so admits a net positive charge.
seeds.objective: Name the ions and channels responsible for phase 1 and phase 2 of the non-pacemaker cardiac action potential, and say why the plateau stays flat.
seeds.pitfall: Reading the plateau as a period without current. It is two large opposing currents cancelling, which is why a small change in either potassium or calcium conductance moves the whole plateau.
seeds.subject: cvs
seeds.modulePath: 104 CPS > Physiology > Cardiovascular System > Electrical Activity of the Heart
aliases: Phase 1 and phase 2 of the ventricular action potential
Ionic basis of the cardiac plateau

seeds.asked: Compare between rapid ejection phase and reduced ejection phase regarding ventricular pressure, ventricular volume, semilunar valves and arterial pressure
seeds.label: Rapid and reduced ejection differ in the pressure gradient and the rate of emptying, not in whether the semilunar valves are open
seeds.definition: Both phases of ventricular ejection run with the semilunar valves open. In rapid ejection the ventricle is still developing force: ventricular pressure rises to its peak, about 120 mmHg on the left and 25 mmHg on the right, arterial pressure rises with it, and ventricular volume falls steeply. In reduced ejection the gradient has reversed and ejection continues only on the momentum of the moving column: ventricular and arterial pressure both fall, and ventricular volume falls slowly to the end-systolic volume of about 60 ml. When the momentum is spent a small backflow produces the dicrotic notch and the valves close.
seeds.objective: Set the two ejection phases side by side for semilunar valve state, ventricular pressure, ventricular volume and arterial pressure.
seeds.pitfall: Expecting ejection to stop the moment ventricular pressure falls below arterial pressure. It continues on momentum, and it is the loss of that momentum, not the crossing of the pressures, that ends it.

seeds.modulePath: 104 CPS > Physiology > Cardiovascular System > Cardiac Function

seeds.asked: Illustrate the effect of increased in inotropy on left ventricle pressure-volume loop
seeds.label: Increased inotropy shifts the end-systolic pressure-volume relation up and to the left, so the loop starts at the same end-diastolic volume and ends at a lower end-systolic volume
seeds.definition: The end-systolic pressure-volume relation is the line on which the upper left corner of every loop lies, and its slope is the ventricle's contractility. A positive inotropic intervention shifts that line upwards and to the left. Contraction still begins at the same end-diastolic volume, so the loop is unchanged on its right-hand edge, but the ventricle now empties to a lower end-systolic volume; the loop is therefore wider and the stroke volume larger at the same preload.
seeds.objective: Draw what increased inotropy does to the ventricular pressure-volume loop, and say which corner of the loop moves and which does not.
seeds.pitfall: Reading the wider loop as a preload effect. Preload moves the right-hand edge of the loop; inotropy moves the end-systolic relation and therefore the left-hand edge.

seeds.modulePath: 104 CPS > Physiology > Cardiovascular System > Cardiac Function

seeds.asked: Explain heart rate reserve and stroke volume reserve
seeds.label: Heart rate reserve runs from about 75/min to 220 minus age, and stroke volume reserve from about 70 ml to 200 ml
seeds.definition: Cardiac reserve is the maximum percentage by which cardiac output can rise above rest. Heart rate reserve is the span between the resting rate of about 75/min and the maximal rate, estimated as 220 minus age in years, about 200/min in a normal young adult. Stroke volume reserve is the span between about 70 ml at rest and up to 200 ml at maximal exercise, obtained by raising end-diastolic volume through Starling's mechanism and by lowering end-systolic volume through positive inotropy.
seeds.objective: Give the range of each reserve and the mechanism by which stroke volume reserve is realised.
seeds.pitfall: Treating maximal heart rate as trainable. Training raises stroke volume reserve and cardiac mass; maximal rate is set by age and does not rise with training.
seeds.subject: cvs
seeds.modulePath: 104 CPS > Physiology > Cardiovascular System > Cardiac Function

seeds.asked: Explain the changes on MSFP on venous return curve
seeds.label: Raising mean systemic filling pressure shifts the venous return curve up and to the right without changing its slope
seeds.definition: Mean systemic filling pressure is the pressure throughout the systemic circulation when the heart has stopped and flow is zero, normally 6 to 8 mmHg, and it is the force that drives blood back to the right atrium. It reflects blood volume against the capacity of the circulation, which is mainly the capacity of the veins: it rises with increased blood volume, as in renal failure, or with reduced capacity, as in sympathetic venoconstriction, and falls with haemorrhage or with sympathetic withdrawal. On the venous return curve a rise in mean systemic filling pressure produces a parallel shift up and to the right, so at any right atrial pressure venous return is greater; a fall shifts the curve down and to the left.
seeds.objective: Say what mean systemic filling pressure is, what changes it, and how a change in it moves the venous return curve.
seeds.pitfall: Confusing this with a change in resistance to venous return, which pivots the curve by changing its slope rather than shifting it in parallel.
seeds.subject: cvs
seeds.modulePath: 104 CPS > Physiology > Cardiovascular System > Vascular Function
aliases: Mean systemic filling pressure on the venous return curve

seeds.asked: Explain how thoracic pump helps in venous return
seeds.label: Inspiration makes intrapleural pressure more negative, lowering right atrial pressure and widening the gradient for venous return
seeds.definition: During inspiration intrapleural pressure falls from about -4 to -8 mmHg. That fall is transmitted to the intrathoracic great veins and the right atrium, so right atrial pressure falls, the gradient between the mean systemic filling pressure and the right atrium widens, and venous return increases. During expiration intrapleural pressure rises from about -8 back to -4 mmHg, right atrial and caval pressures rise with it, the gradient narrows and venous return decreases.
seeds.objective: Explain how the respiratory swing in intrapleural pressure alters venous return in each phase of the breath.
seeds.pitfall: Describing it as the chest sucking blood in. It works by lowering the downstream pressure at the right atrium; the driving pressure is still the mean systemic filling pressure upstream.

seeds.modulePath: 104 CPS > Physiology > Cardiovascular System > Vascular Function

seeds.asked: Explain function of baroreceptors when ABP increases and when it decreases
seeds.label: Baroreceptor discharge rises and falls with arterial pressure and, through the nucleus of the tractus solitarius, opposes whichever change caused it
seeds.definition: Arterial baroreceptors are stretch receptors in the carotid sinus and the aortic arch, reporting to the nucleus of the tractus solitarius through the carotid sinus (Hering's) nerve and the aortic nerve. When arterial pressure rises their discharge increases: the vasomotor area is inhibited more, so sympathetic drive to heart and vessels falls, giving a lower heart rate, stroke volume and cardiac output with vasodilatation; and the cardiac inhibitory area is excited more, so vagal tone rises and the rate falls further. When arterial pressure falls the discharge decreases and every one of those changes reverses, raising the pressure back towards normal.
seeds.objective: State where the arterial baroreceptors sit, which nerves they use, and what each limb of the reflex does when arterial pressure rises and when it falls.
seeds.pitfall: Answering with the atrial volume receptors. Those are low-pressure receptors whose reflex is about volume, not arterial pressure — and that is the answer the solved copy of this paper actually gives.
seeds.subject: cvs
seeds.modulePath: 104 CPS > Physiology > Cardiovascular System > Basic Mechanisms of Circulatory Control

seeds.asked: Mention causes of chest wall to expand and lung to recoil
seeds.label: The lung recoils inward from its elastic tissue and its alveolar surface tension; the chest wall springs outward from its own elasticity
seeds.definition: The lung's inward recoil has two sources: its collagen and elastin fibres, which account for about one third, and the surface tension of the fluid lining the alveoli, which accounts for about two thirds. The chest wall's outward tendency comes from the elasticity of its muscles, tendons and ligaments. Each has a relaxation volume of its own, about 1 litre for the lungs and 5 litres for the thorax, and at the end of a quiet expiration their combined volume is about 2.3 litres — so the lungs are partially stretched and pulling in while the thorax is partially compressed and pushing out. These two opposing pulls are what keep intrapleural pressure negative.
seeds.objective: Give the causes of the lung's recoil tendency and the chest wall's expansion tendency, with the relaxation volume of each.
seeds.pitfall: Giving elastic tissue alone. Surface tension is the larger of the two contributions, which is why surfactant matters so much to the work of breathing.

seeds.modulePath: 104 CPS > Physiology > Respiratory System > Organization of the Respiratory System
aliases: Recoil tendency of the lung and expansion tendency of the chest wall

seeds.asked: Mention functions of surfactants and 4 causes of deficiency of surfactant
seeds.label: Surfactant lowers alveolar surface tension, which eases inflation, prevents alveolar collapse and prevents pulmonary oedema
seeds.definition: Pulmonary surfactant is secreted by type II alveolar cells and lowers the surface tension of the alveolar lining fluid. That does three things: it facilitates lung expansion, so less effort is needed in inspiration; it prevents alveolar collapse in expiration, because as an alveolus shrinks its surfactant molecules crowd closer and lower the surface tension faster than the falling radius raises the collapsing pressure P = 2T/r; and it prevents pulmonary oedema, because surface tension itself favours filtration of fluid from blood into the alveoli. It is deficient in infant respiratory distress syndrome of prematurity, after long inhalation of 100% oxygen or use of a pump oxygenator in cardiac surgery, when a branch of the pulmonary artery is occluded, in cigarette smoking, in hypothyroidism, in hypocorticism and in hyperinsulinism.
seeds.objective: Give the three functions of surfactant and at least four conditions in which it is deficient.
seeds.pitfall: Reading Laplace's law as making the small alveolus empty into the large one. Surfactant is more concentrated in the smaller alveolus, so its surface tension is lower and the law does not apply with a fixed T.
seeds.subject: resp
seeds.modulePath: 104 CPS > Physiology > Respiratory System > Organization of the Respiratory System

seeds.asked: Mention the factors that shift Hb-O2 dissociation curve to the left
seeds.label: A fall in temperature, PCO2 or 2,3-DPG, a rise in pH, carbon monoxide and fetal haemoglobin all shift the curve to the left
seeds.definition: A leftward shift is a lower P50 and a higher affinity of haemoglobin for oxygen, so at any given PO2 more oxygen stays bound and less is delivered. It is produced by a decrease in temperature, a decrease in PCO2 and an increase in pH — the Bohr effect run backwards — by a decrease in 2,3-diphosphoglycerate, by carbon monoxide, which occupies the oxygen-binding sites with more than two hundred times the affinity of oxygen and holds the remaining oxygen more tightly, and by fetal haemoglobin, whose two gamma chains cannot combine with 2,3-DPG.
seeds.objective: List the factors that shift the haemoglobin-oxygen dissociation curve to the left and say what a left shift means for oxygen delivery.
seeds.pitfall: Treating a left shift as good for the tissues. High affinity means the blood loads oxygen well and unloads it badly, which is exactly why carbon monoxide poisoning is dangerous at any measured saturation.
seeds.subject: resp
seeds.modulePath: 104 CPS > Physiology > Respiratory System > Gas Transport by the Blood

seeds.asked: Mention the end of posterior intercoastal and subcostal veins
seeds.label: The posterior intercostal veins end differently on the two sides: on the right directly in the azygos system, on the left through the two hemiazygos veins
seeds.definition: There are eleven posterior intercostal veins and a subcostal vein on each side. On the right the first ends in the right brachiocephalic vein; the second, third and fourth unite as the right superior intercostal vein, which ends in the arch of the azygos vein; and the fifth to eleventh, with the subcostal vein, open separately into the azygos vein. On the left the first ends in the left brachiocephalic vein; the second, third and fourth unite as the left superior intercostal vein, which also ends in the left brachiocephalic vein; the fifth to eighth open into the superior hemiazygos vein, which begins as the continuation of the fifth; and the ninth, tenth and eleventh, with the subcostal vein, open into the inferior hemiazygos vein. Both hemiazygos veins cross the midline to end in the azygos vein.
seeds.objective: Give the termination of each posterior intercostal vein and of the subcostal vein on both sides.
seeds.pitfall: Forgetting the first vein on either side. It joins no part of the azygos system — it goes straight to the brachiocephalic vein, and the solved copy of this paper leaves it out.
seeds.subject: cvs
seeds.modulePath: 104 CPS > Anatomy > Intercostal Spaces

seeds.asked: Mention the nerve supply of pleura
seeds.label: Visceral pleura takes autonomic fibres from the pulmonary plexuses and feels no pain; parietal pleura takes the somatic nerve of the wall it lines and does
seeds.definition: The visceral (pulmonary) pleura is supplied by the same autonomic innervation as the lung, through the anterior and posterior pulmonary plexuses, and is not sensitive to somatic stimuli such as pain and temperature. The parietal pleura takes the somatic innervation of the structure it lines: the cervical pleura from the first intercostal nerve, the costal pleura segmentally from the corresponding intercostal nerve, the mediastinal pleura and the central part of the diaphragmatic pleura from the phrenic nerve, and the peripheral part of the diaphragmatic pleura from the lower intercostal nerves.
seeds.objective: Give the nerve supply of visceral and parietal pleura, naming the nerve for each part of the parietal pleura.
seeds.pitfall: Giving the phrenic nerve the whole diaphragmatic pleura. Only its central part is phrenic; the periphery is intercostal, which is why diaphragmatic irritation refers to the shoulder in one case and to the abdominal wall in the other.
seeds.subject: resp
seeds.modulePath: 104 CPS > Anatomy > Thoracic Cavity

seeds.asked: Mention origin, end and branches of circumflex branch of left coronary artery
seeds.label: The circumflex artery arises at the top of the anterior interventricular groove and ends by anastomosing with the right coronary artery behind
seeds.definition: The circumflex artery is one of the two terminal branches of the left coronary artery, arising at the upper end of the anterior interventricular groove. It passes left in the anterior part of the coronary sulcus, turns round the left border of the heart, and ends in the posterior part of the sulcus by anastomosing with the right coronary artery; the coronary sinus accompanies it, the blood in the two vessels running the same way. Its branches are the left marginal artery, which descends on the left aspect of the heart supplying the left ventricle down to the apex; branches to the left atrium; branches to the anterior and diaphragmatic surfaces of the left ventricle; the artery to the sinu-atrial node in 40% of people; and the artery to the atrioventricular node and bundle in 20%.
seeds.objective: Give the origin, course, termination and named branches of the circumflex artery, including the proportion in which it supplies each node.
seeds.pitfall: Assuming the nodal arteries are always right coronary. The circumflex supplies the sinu-atrial node in 40% and the atrioventricular node in 20%, which is why a circumflex occlusion can present as a bradyarrhythmia.
seeds.subject: cvs
seeds.modulePath: 104 CPS > Anatomy > Heart

seeds.asked: Mention the boundaries and contents of posterior medistinum
seeds.label: The posterior mediastinum lies between pericardium and diaphragm in front and the lower eight thoracic vertebrae behind
seeds.definition: Its boundaries are the pericardium above and the diaphragm below in front, and the lower eight thoracic vertebrae, T5 to T12, behind. Its contents are five groups: the descending thoracic aorta and its branches; the azygos and hemiazygos venous system; the two vagi, which form the oesophageal plexuses, together with the sympathetic trunks and their splanchnic branches; the oesophagus and the thoracic duct, which runs along its right side; and the posterior mediastinal lymph nodes.
seeds.objective: Give the boundaries of the posterior mediastinum and list its contents by group.
seeds.pitfall: Stopping at four groups. The posterior mediastinal lymph nodes are the fifth, and they are the group the solved copy of this paper loses.

seeds.modulePath: 104 CPS > Anatomy > Mediastinum

seeds.asked: Mention fate of aortic sac
seeds.label: The right horn of the aortic sac becomes the brachiocephalic artery; the stem and left horn become the proximal part of the arch of the aorta
seeds.definition: The aortic sac forms when the two ventral aortae fuse after the heart tubes fuse, and consists of a stem with a right and a left horn. Its right horn becomes the brachiocephalic artery, which is continuous with the right common carotid artery from the third aortic arch and the right subclavian artery from the fourth. Its stem and left horn together form the proximal part of the arch of the aorta; the middle part of the arch comes from the left fourth aortic arch and the distal part from the left dorsal aorta.
seeds.objective: Give the adult derivative of the right horn and of the stem and left horn of the aortic sac.
seeds.pitfall: Handing the whole arch of the aorta to the aortic sac. Only its proximal part is sac-derived; the middle is the left fourth aortic arch and the distal is left dorsal aorta.

seeds.asked: An old man suffers from pulsatile retrosternal chest pain which increases following effort associated with irregular heartbeats, dysphagia and horsiness of voice. a. Name the affected organ and the diagnosis of the disease b. Explain the reason of the irregular heart beats c. Explain the reason of the dysphagia e. Why there is horsiness of voice
seeds.label: An aneurysm of the arch of the aorta declares itself through the structures the arch is related to
seeds.definition: A localized dilatation of the arch of the aorta compresses the contents of the superior mediastinum and produces the mediastinal syndrome. The structures it stretches or presses are exactly those related to the arch: the superficial cardiac plexus, on its concavity, so pulling and stretching it gives irregular heartbeats; the oesophagus, behind the arch, so compression gives dysphagia; and the left recurrent laryngeal nerve, hooking under the arch beside the ligamentum arteriosum, so stretching it gives hoarseness of voice. The pain is retrosternal and pulsatile and is worse on effort.
seeds.objective: Recognise an arch aneurysm from a triad of arrhythmia, dysphagia and hoarseness, and name the related structure that produces each.
seeds.pitfall: Blaming the right recurrent laryngeal nerve. It hooks round the right subclavian artery in the neck; only the left one is related to the arch, so an arch lesion gives a left cord palsy.

seeds.asked: Mention the difference between palatine and lingual tonsils as regard the site, epithelial covering and crypt
seeds.label: Palatine and lingual tonsils share a non-keratinized stratified squamous covering but differ in site and in the number of crypts
seeds.definition: The palatine tonsils are paired ovoid masses of lymphoid tissue in the lateral wall of the oropharynx; the lingual tonsils are multiple masses at the posterior third, the base, of the tongue. Both are covered by non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium which dips into the lymphoid tissue as crypts. The palatine tonsil has multiple crypts and the ducts of its mucous glands open on the surface rather than at the crypt bases, so debris accumulates and tonsillitis is common; each lingual tonsil has a single crypt whose base receives the mucous gland ducts, so it is continuously washed and inflammation is uncommon.
seeds.objective: Compare palatine and lingual tonsils by site, epithelial covering and crypts.
seeds.pitfall: Trying to separate them by epithelium. Both are non-keratinized stratified squamous; it is the site and the crypts that tell them apart, and the pharyngeal tonsil is the one with a different epithelium and no crypts at all.
seeds.subject: haem
seeds.modulePath: 104 CPS > Histology > Lymphatic and Macrophage System > Tonsils

seeds.asked: Outline the zones of white pulp and state the cellular composition of each zone
seeds.label: Splenic white pulp is four zones arranged concentrically around the central arteriole
seeds.definition: Each Malpighian corpuscle of the white pulp is reticular connective tissue whose cells are arranged concentrically around an eccentrically placed central arteriole, in four zones from inside outwards. The thymus-dependent zone, the periarteriolar lymphatic sheath, holds T lymphocytes ensheathing the arteriole. The germinal centre is a pale central area of B lymphocytes, large activated lymphocytes, plasma cells and macrophages. The follicular zone is the darkly stained ring around the germinal centre, mainly B lymphocytes. The marginal zone forms the periphery and contains T and B lymphocytes, plasma cells and macrophages.
seeds.objective: Name the four zones of splenic white pulp in order from the central arteriole outwards and give the cells of each.
seeds.pitfall: Taking the central arteriole to be central. It is eccentric in the corpuscle; the name describes the sheath wrapped around it, not its position.
seeds.subject: haem
seeds.modulePath: 104 CPS > Histology > Lymphatic and Macrophage System > Spleen

seeds.asked: Classify the specialized cells according to their ability to reproduce and state one example for each
seeds.label: Specialized cells are non-renewing, potentially renewable, or continuously renewing from stem cells
seeds.definition: Most working specialized cells spend a prolonged G1 and are not in active cycle. Non-renewing cells leave the cycle in G1 for G0 permanently and never divide again, and are not replaced when lost — cardiac muscle and nerve cells. Potentially renewable cells enter G0 but can re-enter the cycle when replacement is needed, a transient exit — liver cells after destruction or partial removal. Continuously renewing cells are end cells that cannot themselves divide but are replaced from stem cells — blood cells and sperms.
seeds.objective: Classify specialized cells by their ability to reproduce and give one example of each class.
seeds.pitfall: Reading 'continuously renewing' as continuously dividing. The end cell does not divide at all; it is the stem cell behind it that does.

seeds.modulePath: 104 CPS > Histology > Cytogenetics > The Cell Cycle

seeds.asked: Outline the causes of aneuploidy
seeds.label: Aneuploidy arises from non-disjunction, from failure of duplication, or from simple loss of a chromosome
seeds.definition: Aneuploidy is a chromosome number that is not an exact multiple of the haploid number, the karyotype having gained or lost a single chromosome. It arises from non-disjunction, primary when two homologous chromosomes fail to separate at the first meiotic division, giving four abnormal daughter cells, and secondary when two chromatids fail to separate at the centromere at the second meiotic division or in mitosis, giving two normal and two abnormal daughter cells in meiosis and two abnormal cells in mitosis; from failure of duplication, one chromatid failing to duplicate in S phase; and from simple loss, a chromosome failing to align at metaphase or lagging in anaphase. Secondary non-disjunction occurring in mitosis after many normal divisions produces a mosaic, whose body cells carry more than one karyotype.
seeds.objective: Give the causes of aneuploidy, distinguishing primary from secondary non-disjunction by the daughter cells each produces.
seeds.pitfall: Treating aneuploidy as always meiotic. Mitotic non-disjunction after fertilisation gives mosaicism, which is why a karyotype from one tissue can read normal in an affected patient.

seeds.modulePath: 104 CPS > Histology > Cytogenetics > Chromosomal Aberrations (Abnormalities)

seeds.asked: Describe the histological characteristics of the somatic and sinusoidal capillaries regarding endothelium, junctions and basal lamina state one site for each
seeds.label: Continuous capillaries are sealed tubes on a continuous basal lamina; sinusoids are wide, porous and discontinuous
seeds.definition: A continuous (somatic) capillary is small and regular in calibre; its endothelium is continuous with no pores, its endothelial cells are joined by tight junctions, and its basal lamina is continuous. It is found all over the body — connective tissue, bone, skin, exocrine glands. A sinusoidal capillary, or blood sinusoid, is large and irregular; its endothelium has pores without diaphragms, its endothelial cells are separated by wide intercellular spaces rather than sealed by tight junctions, and its basal lamina is non-continuous. It is found in the liver, carrying plasma proteins, in endocrine glands, carrying hormones, in bone marrow, carrying formed blood cells, and in the spleen, carrying stored blood cells.
seeds.objective: Contrast continuous and sinusoidal capillaries by endothelium, intercellular junctions and basal lamina, and give one site for each.
seeds.pitfall: Confusing a sinusoid with a fenestrated capillary. Both have pores, but the fenestrated capillary's pores are covered by diaphragms and its basal lamina is continuous.
seeds.subject: cvs
seeds.modulePath: 104 CPS > Histology > Cardiovascular System > A-V Connections

seeds.asked: Compare between respiratory mucosa and olfactory mucosa as regard the epithelial thickness, basement membrane. cilia and goblet cells
seeds.label: Olfactory mucosa is the thicker epithelium on the thinner basement membrane, with few long immotile cilia and no goblet cells
seeds.definition: The olfactory mucosa covers the roof and the superior conchae of the nasal cavity. Its epithelium is much thicker than respiratory epithelium and rests on a thin basement membrane; it has no goblet cells, and its cilia are few, very long and non-motile, arising from the olfactory vesicle to enlarge the surface exposed to odorants. Respiratory mucosa has a thinner epithelium on a thick basement membrane, numerous true motile cilia, and goblet cells. Olfactory mucosa also carries Bowman's glands and the yellow lipofuscin pigment of its sustentacular cells; respiratory mucosa has neither.
seeds.objective: Compare respiratory and olfactory mucosa by epithelial thickness, basement membrane, cilia and goblet cells.
seeds.pitfall: Calling the olfactory cilia motile. They do not beat; they are receptive processes lying in the serous fluid of Bowman's glands, which is where odorants dissolve.
